content: Niigata Minamata disease has been officially recognized in 690 individuals from the Agano River basin. This outbreak, which occurred in the lower Agano River basin, was the second recorded instance of Minamata disease in Japan, following the original outbreak in Kumamoto Prefecture. It is one of Japan's Four Big Pollution Diseases. The second outbreak of Minamata disease in Niigata Prefecture was discovered in a manner similar to the original outbreak. A cat exhibited unusual symptoms, including dilated pupils, excessive salivation, convulsions, and strange vocalizations, before succumbing to its condition. These symptoms were later observed in humans as well. In April and May 1965, Professor Tadao Tsubaki of Niigata University examined two patients and suspected Minamata disease. Analysis of one patient’s hair revealed a mercury concentration of 390 ppm. On May 31, 1965, Professor Tsubaki reported an outbreak of organic mercury poisoning in the Agano River basin to the prefectural government and made his findings public on June 12. During 1965 and 1966, researchers from the Kumamoto University Research Group, which had previously investigated the original Minamata outbreak, and Dr. Hajime Hosokawa, the former director of Chisso Hospital, applied their expertise to the Niigata outbreak. Lessons learned from the Minamata case allowed the investigation in Niigata to proceed more efficiently. Collaboration among the prefectural government, Niigata University, citizen organizations, and local residents helped identify the cause of the outbreak. By March 1966, factory wastewater was suspected as the source of pollution, and in September, the Ministry of Health and Welfare announced the discovery of methylmercury in moss samples collected at the outlet of the Showa Denko factory in Kanose village. Showa Denko, the company implicated in the Niigata outbreak, responded similarly to how Chisso had reacted in Minamata. The company attempted to discredit researchers and proposed alternative theories, such as agricultural chemical runoff entering the river after the 1964 Niigata earthquake, as the cause of the disease. Showa Denko distributed informational leaflets rejecting the claim that their wastewater was responsible for the outbreak. Unlike the victims in Minamata, those affected by Showa Denko’s pollution lived far from the factory and had no direct connection to the company. This geographical separation led to stronger support from the local community for the patients’ groups. In March 1968, a lawsuit was filed against Showa Denko, just three years after the outbreak was made public in 1965. In contrast, the first lawsuit in Minamata was filed in 1969, thirteen years after the initial outbreak was discovered. On September 26, 1968, the government officially concluded that the Niigata Minamata disease was likely caused by mercury discharged from the Kanose plant over an extended period. However, the report did not entirely rule out other potential causes, and Showa Denko’s president, Masao Yasunishi, continued to deny the company’s responsibility. The Niigata lawsuit ultimately succeeded, and on September 29, 1971, the court found Showa Denko guilty of negligence. Compensation was awarded to the victims: families of deceased and congenital patients received JPY 10 million (approximately USD 28,600), surviving patients were awarded between JPY 1 million and JPY 10 million depending on the severity of their symptoms, individuals contaminated by mercury received JPY 400,000 (approximately USD 1,145), and pregnant women advised to have abortions due to the risk to their unborn children were awarded JPY 300,000 (approximately USD 858). The events in Niigata prompted a reevaluation of the original Minamata incident. The scientific research conducted in Niigata led to a reexamination of earlier studies in Minamata, and the decision of Niigata patients to sue the polluting company set a precedent for similar actions in Minamata. These developments catalyzed significant changes in the response to industrial pollution and its consequences in Japan.
